text:
Norman Swan: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, a worm treatment for asthma that you should be able to
stomach, saving a fortune on medications by getting around the negative placebo
effect, the nocebo, and how behavioural problems in people with dementia
should be treated but rarely are, and peeing razorblades. A casual glance around
the supplement shelves in your local pharmacy will tell you that cranberry extract
is extremely popular. It's used by women mostly when they have cystitis or a
urinary infection, but a recent randomised trial suggests you might be best saving
your money. The person who led the study was Manisha Jutani-Mehta, an
infectious disease physician and researcher at Yale University's School of
Medicine.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: The history of cranberry is quite old in the United
States. Cranberry is one of the few native fruits in North America, and Native
Americans used cranberries for a variety of sources for thousands of years.
Whether it be for bartering, for dye, to use as a vitamin C supplement, and they
used it for a variety of health ailments. And so when the first settlers came to
America, at that time the pilgrims adopted cranberry and starting using it to barter
in Europe and also started using it for some of the same purposes that Native
Americans used it for. That's why cranberries are such an integral part of our
American Thanksgiving and of…

Norman Swan: I was going to say that, so it adds symbolism to the Thanksgiving
turkey.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Absolutely and that really goes back to that initial
sharing of the foods that were native to North America, new to many of the
settlers who had arrived. And so the settlers really learned the ways of the Native
Americans. And as in most cultures, people use things that are around them that
they have access to for a variety of conditions. If you look at any ancient tradition
they use things that were around them for a variety of health ailments, and things
were used that were thought to be helpful in one way or another. And in modern
medicine many of these things are true, many of these things may not be quite
true but for whatever reason we've adopted different things in our social culture
to suit the purposes that we use them for. So I think in American culture the
history of cranberry goes back to that.
 
And if we then look at cranberry history and cranberry research since that time, it
extends into the early 1900s when the first scientific reports of why cranberry
juice might be helpful for urinary tract infections start coming out. And at that time
the initial thoughts were that cranberry juice acidified the urine and that was how
it prevented urinary tract infections.

I think one of the other major differences and one of the concepts that I think
people have to realise is that there are two things we tried to do for UTIs. One is
to try to prevent them. And the second is to try to treat them. Most of the studies
that have been done using cranberry products has been done to try to prevent
urinary tract infection.

What I think probably is true…I don't have proof of this but I have a feeling that
the Native Americans used it for this purpose as well and that's how the early
pilgrims and settlers did the same, which is that I believe cranberry juice probably
does have some anti-inflammatory effect or an effect that we're not quite sure
how it works, but it does reduce the burning sensation that women have when
they are developing a UTI. This is what many women anecdotally say cranberry
juice helps them for.

And so I think that when people start developing the UTI, so now we're going into
the realm of treatment, not prevention, that cranberry juice seems to ease those
symptoms. It does not treat the UTI, and I know women who have started taking
cranberry juice and the bladder infection goes on and progresses to a kidney
infection because the symptoms go away. But I think that that distinction is one
that is important for people to realise. And I think that that is somewhat blurred in
terms of the old wives' tales and the tradition of cranberry that exists in America
and therefore around the world as well. And what our study looked at really was
more about prevention, and that's what most of the studies that are in the
scientific literature are about, is about prevention of UTI with cranberry products.

Norman Swan: So tell us what you did in the study.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: So in our study I really tried to replicate the findings of
the first juice study that was in a strong way positive in older women. So this was
going back to 1994, a study published in the Journal of the American Medical
Association, JAMA, that looked at older women living in nursing homes and
 
assisted living facilities, and it looked at 10 ounces of cranberry juice cocktail to
prevent bacteria and white cells in the urine. The problem with cranberry juice is
that for many women it has a very acrid flavour, they can't drink the volume that
is necessary, they don't like the load of sugar that potentially could be with it. And
so for these reasons, even though that study was a positive study in that
population, many women are just unable to do that. And so for that reason in our
study I looked at the equivalent of 20 ounces of cranberry juice cocktail. So I
looked at two capsules. The capsule that we used had 36 milligrams of the
equivalent of proanthocyanidin, or a tannin which is in cranberry juice cocktail
that is thought to be the active ingredient in preventing UTIs…

Norman Swan: And in fact in the laboratory it has been shown to stop the
stickiness of the E. coli, the bug that causes the urinary tract infections, stops it
sticking to the surface lining of the urinary tract in the laboratory.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: That's exactly right. And so in the lab studies they have
been shown to inhibit binding to the bladder wall cells. In fact we used pilot data
from a previous study, and this is a compound we then used, that actually looks
at the urine of women who ingested various levels and doses of that active
ingredient and saw that there was decreased binding with increases in dose. And
so we ended up using 72 milligrams a pack, which was double the dose that was
shown the 1994 study, and the thought there was that in our pilot data we had
seen that 72 milligrams was more effective than 36 milligrams in these older
women. And my thought was that maybe by reducing the hydration we needed a
higher dose. And so that was the dose we then tested, and we enrolled 185
women who lived in nursing homes, followed them for one year and checked
their urine for bacteria and white cells in the urine every two months over the
course of that year.

Norman Swan: And you also checked them for symptomatic infections, in other
words whether they were getting burning and discomfort.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Yes exactly.

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: So we did check them for symptomatic infections as
well. One of the big challenges with that though is that in older women those
 
types of symptoms are very uncommon. So in our older overall findings we did
not find a difference or a reduction in bacteria or white blood cells in the urine of
these women over the course of one year.

Over that same one-year period of time, we only had 10 symptomatic UTIs in the
treatment group and 12 in the control group, so we really can't say too much
about that because we weren't powered to detect the difference for symptomatic
UTI. What we were powered for was to look at this difference between bacteria
and white cells in the urine.

Norman Swan: And when you say powered, you mean the number of people
that you had in your study versus the kind of effect that you were looking for.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Right. So to clarify that, whenever you are designing a
study you're trying to figure out what is the effect that we are anticipating these
cranberry capsules are going to have, and based on that '94 study we were
expecting a certain reduction, a 33% relative reduction in the amount of bacteria
and white cells in the urine. So based on that and based on the baseline
prevalence of bacteria and white cells in the urine to start with, we came up with
a calculation that we needed to have at least 180 patients in this trial. And we
were actually able to enrol 185, so a little bit more than what we were expecting.
Nevertheless, we still were not able to show a difference.

Norman Swan: So just to pick this apart just a little bit and briefly, you could
argue that not taking the juice loses the hydrating effect, the flushing effect. So in
other words maybe it is the cranberries plus flushing that works here rather than
the extract by itself. So I am a firm believer that the hydration is absolutely
necessary in terms of UTI prevention. Having said that, if we look at the bulk of
studies that have been done in multiple different populations, it's been shown that
cranberry juice products overall do not seem to be working. The body of
evidence would basically suggest, even in the juice studies, that cranberry versus
placebo juice alone even still did not have an effect. So one of the interesting
things is one study that was done looked at cranberry juice versus placebo. And
in both groups the rate of UTI went down.

Norman Swan: But it was because of the fluid.
 
Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Right, exactly. That would suggest that the hydration
alone was sufficient in that population. So one of the challenges of our study is
can we say that it is generalisable to all audiences, to all potential patients? And
the one thing I would say is we didn't test all potential groups. We did test older,
debilitated, frail women who were living in nursing homes. But aside from my
study, another review that looked at all the studies that have been done over the
last many years, so a Cochrane review that was done in 2012 actually also had
come to a similar conclusion that data to date does not suggest that cranberry
products are actually effective at preventing UTI.

Norman Swan: Which is a shame, because it would reduce the rate of use of
antibiotics.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Absolutely, and that's the main reason I did the study
in the first place is because nursing home residents are exposed to antibiotics so
frequently and they are at risk for infection, so much so that I was hoping that a
non-antimicrobial method would be possible at preventing UTIs in these
unfortunate women. But we did not find that. And hydration is challenging in
these women. Hydration, although it is strongly recommended, it is challenging.

Norman Swan: So where does that leave a younger woman, say, who is having
recurrent cystitis, driven nuts by it, if this is applicable to her, then cranberry
extract is probably not going to make a big difference to preventing cystitis. And
this is also a group of women who are overexposed to antibiotics, at least in the
Australian setting and I suspect in the American as well, the wrong antibiotics for
the wrong length of time. Just give us a potted story for the woman with recurrent
cystitis, because it's an incredibly painful condition.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: It absolutely is, and I think that although this study
really can't comment on that because the younger woman who is having
recurrent cystitis is a different type of patient. But what I would say is that for
those women, there are probably a few things that may help and are very low
risk. So for the younger woman, post coital voiding can help prevent having a
UTI.

Norman Swan: So going to the bathroom after you've had sex.
 
Manisha Juthani-Mehta: That's correct, so going to the bathroom, urinating after
you've had sex can certainly be one thing that is easy to do and potentially could
reduce the number of UTIs you have. The second thing I have told many women
and I have seen anecdotally a lot of success is that women who really are strict
about the amount of fluids they take every day, so they carry around a large litre
water bottle and refill it as they are done and really push hydration all day long, I
have seen women that are very successful at preventing UTIs. It is a hard thing
to do, I won't deny that, but I think that that is a possibility.

Norman Swan: And if you do need antibiotics, I think that short courses…I think
that if you catch it early and you can take a short course, meaning a three-day
course to treat your urinary tract infection, that's probably your best case to
prevent getting a more complicated urinary tract infection. The other thing that we
do do sometimes for the younger woman who has had three UTIs in a year or
maybe two in six months and is just very debilitated by these recurrent cystitis
episodes is we can sometimes use a chronic suppressive antibiotic. It is not our
choice, it's not our agent of choice, it's not our method of choice. But if somebody
has really suffered a lot and really is looking for another method, that is one thing
that we can do.

Norman Swan: But nobody has researched the man in this, their partner, and
surely it makes sense that they are being reinfected by their partner, and we tend
to focus on investigations of the woman rather than looking at the partner to see
whether the partner is carrying something, and essentially it is a sexually
transmissible infection.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: That is certainly a possibility. I do think though that in
women the closeness of the rectum, the vagina, the urethra allows for the
bacteria that are in your own system to then colonise your own urethra and then
for the bacteria to travel up to the bladder and actually cause an infection. Having
said that, I do think that partners probably do share some of the same bacteria.
So it may or may not be that it is a sexually transmitted disease, rather that we
start seeing that couples share the same type of bacteria that is in the gut that
then can cause infections in the urinary system. And I think that that is the bigger
problem for younger women. I think younger women are often told to wipe from
front to back, this is the reason why, because again, you're trying to prevent
colonisation and infection with your own bacteria from getting into your own
 
bladder. And I think that's the real challenge for younger women who face this
problem.

I can speak for the United States, I'm not sure how this translates to Australia,
but in the United States, cranberry capsules are not a regulated industry, in the
sense that there is not clear oversight on the exact contents and what products
can say are in them and what they can say the effect is. I think that cranberry
juice, many women will tell me that it works for them. And for those who tell me
that I say continue using it. There is little downside to doing that.

Cranberry capsules on the other hand I think are a different category of product
because this is really an unregulated industry. It is an industry which has great
financial potential for companies, but it also is an industry where there is little
upside other than the health benefits. It's not like eating cranberry products or
drinking cranberry products or maybe at least you can enjoy them and maybe
say that there is a benefit in terms of the fact that you like ingesting them.
Capsules are actually very different in that way. And so I'm a little bit more
reluctant, especially based on our findings, to recommend women to take
capsules. Having said that, if they enjoy drinking cranberry juice or taking other
cranberry products, I encourage people to do that, even if they feel it does help
them in preventing UTIs, though the data would suggest it might not.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much indeed for joining us.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Thank you so much for having me.

Norman Swan: And supplements are not very well regulated here either.
Manisha Juthani-Mehta is an infectious physician and researcher at Yale
University's School of Medicine. And a longer version of that interview with a lot
more detail will be available for podcast from the Health Report's website. And
you are listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC news radio and CBC
radio across Canada.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a condition where the body's immune system attacks the
lining of joints, and if untreated can cause serious strife. It's more common than
you might think, and in recent years new medications have come onto the market
which specifically target the immune problem. The trouble is they cost tens of
thousands of dollars a year, when one of the alternative medications,
 
methotrexate, costs a tiny fraction. But according to a piece in today's Medical
Journal of Australia, doctors feed what's called the nocebo effect and convince
people that methotrexate is a dreadful drug. One of the authors is a
rheumatologist, Professor Inam Haq of the University of Sydney and he's with me
now. Welcome to the Health Report.

Inam Haq: Many thanks.

Norman Swan: So what is the nocebo effect?

Inam Haq: So I think that's when there's anticipation of adverse effects from a
medication through information that the patient may receive themselves or from
other people which may then reduce the efficacy of that drug or actually cause it
to be discontinued earlier than might be expected.

Norman Swan: As opposed to the placebo effect…

Inam Haq: Which is a positive.

Norman Swan: Where you expect positive results.

Inam Haq: That's right.

Norman Swan: What we're talking about here are called disease modifying anti-
rheumatoid drugs, or DMARDs, so these are actual ones that affect the disease
itself, and methotrexate is one of them. What are the myths around methotrexate
that doctors perpetuate in your view that make this nocebo effect come into
effect?

Inam Haq: The common one that patients can get, it could be from doctors, other
health professionals or from the internet or other colleagues, is that it's cancer,
that they are being treated for cancer. Because methotrexate at much higher
doses is used to treat various different types of cancer. But we use methotrexate
in a much lower dose, we use it by tablet or injection and we give it weekly.

Norman Swan: And that suggests then it's a very strong treatment.
 
Inam Haq: That's right, so patients can then think, oh my goodness, all my hair
will fall out and all the perceptions that people feel about what chemotherapy can
do.

Norman Swan: And there's also drug interactions which are not really a problem
which people might think is a problem which are also used in rheumatoid arthritis.

Inam Haq: That's right. So, often patients with rheumatoid arthritis who have
inflammation in their joints are given anti-inflammatory medications to help some
of the symptoms. And often a pharmacist and other health professionals say you
can't take those two drugs together. You can. You have to look at the patient
individually and make sure that there are no other reasons why they can't take it.
For example, if they had a stomach ulcer or whether their kidneys are functioning
all right. But overall there is nothing wrong with taking those drugs for short
periods of time.

Norman Swan: And then there is a notion that you don't want to actually share
bodily fluids with somebody on methotrexate because you might get the toxicity
too.

Inam Haq: Yes, that's right. The amount of drug that is actually excreted in bodily
tissues is negligible. So the chance of somebody getting methotrexate toxicity
from somebody else is highly unusual…

Norman Swan: Including pregnant women?

Inam Haq: So pregnant women shouldn't take the drug because it affects
dividing cells and can cause mutations in embryos and so on. So pregnant
women with arthritis shouldn't be taking the drug. But if you are a pregnant
woman in contact with somebody else, normal personal hygiene precautions are
absolutely fine.

Norman Swan: And you don't take this by injection, do you?

Inam Haq: Most people will have it via tablet once a week. For those people in
whom there are side-effects, most commonly nausea or abdominal discomfort,
you can give it by injection just under the skin.

Norman Swan: So there's a bit of a mythology about that too.
 
Inam Haq: That's right. It's interesting, because in other countries in the world
you can get it as a prepackaged injection, rather like a pen injection, which is
very simple, very easy and you can dispose of it very simply. In Australia that
isn't yet available, so it has to be prepared in a hospital, and it's prepared
according to…the standards of much higher doses of methotrexate that you
would use in chemotherapy. So there's a lot of fear around it.

Norman Swan: So what evidence is there that this mythology about
methotrexate…and we are just choosing this almost as an example, does create
side-effects and bad results?

Inam Haq: Well, I think I've had that in my personal practice. Since being in the
country I have had several patients who we've had a discussion around
methotrexate as the gold standard. It's an extremely effective drug, used well and
used correctly and used safely, at reducing joint inflammation and damage. And
I've given patients information and then we have…we get patients back to have a
discussion and they say, 'I'm not very keen, I've read about the side-effects, I've
looked things up,' or they may have heard from other people who are on the
drug. And that then leads to a rather difficult…you know, you're trying to catch up
the whole time, trying to emphasise the important positives of the drug and the
benefits versus some of the perceptions that people may have, that they've heard
from other people.

Norman Swan: I take it from your accent you worked in the UK.

Inam Haq: That's right.

Norman Swan: Were more people on methotrexate in the UK than here?

Inam Haq: No, I think it's probably a similar problem all over, yes.

Norman Swan: So we could save a lot of money here by putting people on
methotrexate if we set people's expectations correctly.

Inam Haq: I think we need to ensure that people go to the right sources of
information. For example, Arthritis Australia has fantastic patient related
information. I think we also need to educate our other healthcare providers,
 
general practitioners for example, practice nurses, to understand better that
methotrexate is not an unusual drug, it is actually the gold standard.

Norman Swan: But just in general, you can understand doctors being a bit
careful here because they've got to take informed consent and they want to
inform people about what side-effects are, but what you're saying is that by
informing people about side-effects you actually might create the side-effect.

Inam Haq: That's right. So it's actually quite a nuanced conversation that you
have to have with the patient around the severity and frequency of those effects
versus the undoubted and proven benefits of methotrexate at reducing joint
damage, inflammation and symptoms to allow that person to carry on with their
normal life.

Norman Swan: And some people have said that statins are the same thing, the
cholesterol lowering drugs, that you are led to expect muscle pain so you get
muscle pain.

Inam Haq: That's right, absolutely, you become hypervigilant as to what bodily
symptoms you have and may attribute them wrongly.

Norman Swan: So you've got to get that fine balance between informed consent
and realism.

Inam Haq: That's right. I think that's actually quite a difficult task and quite a
complex cognitive process.

Norman Swan: If you've got rheumatoid arthritis, do consider methotrexate…

Inam Haq: Very much so, it's a fantastic drug.

Norman Swan: And save the nation's economy. Inam Haq, thanks very much for
joining us.

Inam Haq: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Inam Haq is a rheumatologist at the University of Sydney. He's
also co-director of the Sydney University medical program.
 
There is pretty good evidence that if you are infected with a parasite in your early
childhood you are much less likely to develop asthma. The infection seems to
train your immune system to be less allergic. But most of us would probably
prefer asthma to a dose of worms. But that hasn't stopped a group of researchers
at James Cook University in Far North Queensland looking for a therapy based
on hookworms, and they may have found one.

Severine Navarro is a senior research fellow at James Cook and is in our Cairns
studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Severine Navarro: Hi, thank you so much for having me.

Norman Swan: So there's been…I've noticed just reading up for this, that in fact
there's been a randomised trial of in fact a certain kind of pin worm for asthma
already, the real worm.

Severine Navarro: Yes, but pin worm is different from hook worm…

Norman Swan: Sorry, whip worm rather, not pin worm, yes.

Severine Navarro: Yes, and whip worm as well, it was in a clinical trial, so for
inflammatory bowel disease. It was just not the right kind of worm.

Norman Swan: And not all worms…in terms of the epidemiology, looking at
populations, not all worm infections seem to reduce the risk of asthma. So it's not
every worm.

Severine Navarro: Absolutely, and some may actually even make it worse. But
what's interesting about the…

Norman Swan: Which ones make it worse, just in case we are exposed to them?

Severine Navarro: Oh, many different ones. Usually endemic countries where
you have multiple infections you will have different types of worms that will co-
infect the same host, and it's hard to pinpoint but some are definitely usually
emphasising the pro-allogenic type responses which are called T-helper 2s, and
all this will increase the discomfort and the allergenicity of different types of
allergens to the patient.
 
Norman Swan: And this is infection in the first year of life we're talking about,
isn't it?

Severine Navarro: No, actually it can be just about at any stage. There are
multiple studies that have been showing that children, young children but not
necessarily infants, when they get their worm removed with deworming medicine,
they start to have wheezing and sensitisation appearing. And this is when we
found a relationship between hook worm and allergy.

Norman Swan: In what way?

Severine Navarro: Well, that's the thing. So endemic areas where hook worm
infections are predominant, when you have migration of population, so that's
talking mainly about developing countries, but when you have the migration of
populations from rural to urban areas where they get access to better sanitation
and medication and get the opportunity to obviously get rid of their parasite
infections, a lot of people have suddenly been suffering from autoimmune
diseases and allergy.

Norman Swan: So that made you look at hook worm. And you've discovered this
chemical, this messenger, if you like, that seems to be the key.

Severine Navarro: Well, maybe not the key but a key for sure. It seems for the
public in general it will be definitely more appealing to take a pill than to just
swallow a capsule full of parasites.

Norman Swan: It takes a bit of thought, but you might be right.

Severine Navarro: The thing though is that in my personal opinion it's not just
adults that suffer from asthma, it's also very young children, and I can't imagine
having a young child on corticosteroids. If there is anything that we can do to
prevent this type of medication and help, I think that's the key.

Norman Swan: So this anti-inflammatory protein that you discovered, what does
it do?

Severine Navarro: Well, that's what's actually quite interesting about this protein,
and that's what…it's totally unprecedented, is that it seems like it is
reprogramming certain key cells that are defective in autoimmune and allergy
 
patients. And this sort of reprogramming is resetting the immune response the
right way and suppressing the immune responses that you have in allergen to
immunity.

Norman Swan: Protein obviously comes from the look worm. So obviously
you've got to test this further in animals and then in humans, but if this works, is it
going to be like hook worm infection where you've got to have it for life otherwise
if you stop this treatment you could get a nasty resurgence of your asthma or
allergy?

Severine Navarro: No, absolutely not. So the work that we've done, all the
preclinical work that we've already established, we've seen that a single course
of treatment which so far we've only established to be just a single uptake for 4 to
5 days will protect an organism for up to 14 weeks. So this was done in a study in
mice, so I don't know exactly how we can translate to humans yet. But that
means in terms of previous research done on small animals and asthma, it's
actually a really long time. So that would give the prospect of people just taking
maybe one little course of treatment for a few days, might be protected for
several months.

Norman Swan: And is there any prospect that this could treat autoimmune
disease, like diabetes and other conditions?

Severine Navarro: Possibly. We are currently investigating rheumatoid arthritis.
But the mechanism of action of this particular protein seems to indicate that it
might actually be applicable to multiple other pathologies.

Norman Swan: I hope you have patented it?

Severine Navarro: Oh, we have! But this is a great opportunity for us actually
because it's only with partnering with the industry or willing investors that we can
actually bring this molecule forward and hopefully sooner rather than later on the
market.

Norman Swan: Well, good luck with it, Severine, lots of people will be grateful for
a new treatment that might be so effective.

Severine Navarro: Thank you so much, and that's our reward.
 
Norman Swan: Thanks very much indeed. Severine Navarro is a senior
research fellow at James Cook University and was in our Cairns studio in Far
North Queensland.

Visiting Australia this week is a leading US gerontologist Dr Allen Power. He's
here to convince those caring for people with dementia that is often a better way
than drugs to control what can be very difficult behaviours. Allen Power is in our
Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Allen Power: Thank you so much for having me Norman.

Norman Swan: What are these behaviours?

Allen Power: Well, I'm going to step even away from the word 'behaviours'. I
think that what we have, what I learned, I've worked nearly two decades fulltime
in residential care, used antipsychotic and other drugs were people who are
distressed, and I think the predominant model we've been taught about dementia
has really focused on disease, neuropathology, and it's very reductionistic and
very focused on deficits. And as a result when somebody is distressed or
expresses themselves in other ways it is seen as a difficult behaviour, it is seen
as something that rests with that damaged brain, and that has led us into whole
paradigms like saying behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia that
really put the fault with the person. And if you really think that brain disease is the
root cause, then it's a slippery slope to using medications.

Norman Swan: So if it's not the disease, what's the cause?

Allen Power: Well, I had to step outside that and I had to say, you know,
neuropathology exists but it is part of a much larger thing and that is that it's
within the realm of the individual in how that individual experiences the disease
process. And so I focused on experience instead of just plain pathology, and
came to understand that there is so much more that we don't see, which is the
relational, historical and environmental factors around a person. And that really
we're talking about does the person have well-being, and are there things
between their illness and the way we care for them that may actually erode those
aspects of well-being.

Norman Swan: Be specific, tell us a story then.
 
Allen Power: A perfect example is if you or I living without a diagnosis of
dementia were brought to a shower room by somebody we had never met
before, our clothes were removed and we were showered in a way that maybe
we didn't prefer, with water that maybe had temperature not to our liking, that
would probably bother us. You or I might complain, we might refuse to continue.
A person with dementia who maybe can't remember or express themselves or
cope with the stressors, might shout or strike out. So there's a different response,
the dementia has become an enabler of their distress, but it wasn't the root
cause. The root cause was the way the shower was presented. And when we
blame it on the dementia, then we don't look deeper and we don't find what's
really missing.

Norman Swan: But what you've just described is probably more appropriate for
residential aged care. Plenty of people with dementia are at home and their
partners caring for them find that their behaviours can be very difficult;
aggression, wandering, sleep reversal, there are all sorts of things that happen
that when they desperately want to keep their loved one at home and up in aged
care because that's the only place for them. And as you say, the temptation is to
put them on very strong life-reducing drugs like antipsychotics.

Allen Power: Yes, so let's go to the home for a moment and let's take it out of
residential care. I've worked for years in the culture change field, mainly through
the Eden Alternative and Greenhouse models that came from the US, and what
we've learned is that an institution isn't a building, it's a mindset, it's a way of
operating. And when I look at dementia from the lens of these aspects of well-
being, and in this case I'm talking about seven domains—identity,
connectedness, security, autonomy, meaning, growth, joy.

Let's talk about autonomy for a moment. It is just as easy for a caring family
member who is taught the stigma that the person is fading away, that they are
incapable, to take away autonomy from a family member as well. So it is just as
likely that a person may react to that type of situation in their own home as they
do in a care home. And a perfect example of how institutional practices
transfer…one of the best ways to help a person who has memory loss is not to
rotate staff. It's constant in residential care that people are presented with, to
them, strangers to provide very personal care. Well, even in home care this
happens. My friend Sally Magnusson who is with BBC Glasgow wrote a book
 
about her mother's life, and interviewed the woman whose father lived at home,
and over the course of the year he had 106 different home health workers come
to his house to provide personal care. So these institutional practices happen
everywhere.

Norman Swan: But in an era where there are more and more people with
dementia, even though dementia rates are probably tailing off, is it practical to
give this sort of individual care, particularly in residential care?

Allen Power: It is practical but it requires…that's the third part. So I mentioned
the experiential focus, I mentioned the well-being focus, the third part in this
comes from my culture change backgrounds, this transforming the care system,
because it's not so much about uncaring people or even uneducated people, it's
about a system that still pushes them to focus on tasks, to focus on speed and to
blame the person instead of understanding all the subtle features of the care
environment that actually are causing more distress than the person needs to
have.

Norman Swan: So if your loved one is going into residential aged care, this is a
complete nightmare for people, how do you choose the right place for your loved
one, what are the hallmarks that you should be looking for in a residential aged
care facility?

Allen Power: I think the hallmarks are really to take…almost to close your eyes.
Forget about how pretty the lobby is. See what it feels like, see how people
speak to each other, see how they speak to people living with dementia and see
if they really are focused on the relationship, on the person. That really is where
the key is. The payoff is I work with organisations in the US that have actually not
only severely reduced but eliminated antipsychotic use. So if this really is just a
problem with brain disease, how can you explain somebody who goes from 30%
antipsychotics to zero and keeps it there for a long period of time.

Norman Swan: And ask them about the rosters to see about the consistency.
Allen Power, thank you.

Allen Power's books will be on our website. You've been listening to the Health
Report, I'm Norman Swan. See you next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, a worm treatment for asthma that you should be able to
stomach, saving a fortune on medications by getting around the negative placebo
effect, the nocebo, and how behavioural problems in people with dementia
should be treated but rarely are, and peeing razorblades. A casual glance around
the supplement shelves in your local pharmacy will tell you that cranberry extract
is extremely popular. It's used by women mostly when they have cystitis or a
urinary infection, but a recent randomised trial suggests you might be best saving
your money. The person who led the study was Manisha Jutani-Mehta, an
infectious disease physician and researcher at Yale University's School of
Medicine.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: The history of cranberry is quite old in the United
States. Cranberry is one of the few native fruits in North America, and Native
Americans used cranberries for a variety of sources for thousands of years.
Whether it be for bartering, for dye, to use as a vitamin C supplement, and they
used it for a variety of health ailments. And so when the first settlers came to
America, at that time the pilgrims adopted cranberry and starting using it to barter
in Europe and also started using it for some of the same purposes that Native
Americans used it for. That's why cranberries are such an integral part of our
American Thanksgiving and of…

Norman Swan: I was going to say that, so it adds symbolism to the Thanksgiving
turkey.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Absolutely and that really goes back to that initial
sharing of the foods that were native to North America, new to many of the
settlers who had arrived. And so the settlers really learned the ways of the Native
Americans. And as in most cultures, people use things that are around them that
they have access to for a variety of conditions. If you look at any ancient tradition
they use things that were around them for a variety of health ailments, and things
were used that were thought to be helpful in one way or another. And in modern
medicine many of these things are true, many of these things may not be quite
true but for whatever reason we've adopted different things in our social culture
to suit the purposes that we use them for. So I think in American culture the
history of cranberry goes back to that.

And if we then look at cranberry history and cranberry research since that time, it
extends into the early 1900s when the first scientific reports of why cranberry
juice might be helpful for urinary tract infections start coming out. And at that time
the initial thoughts were that cranberry juice acidified the urine and that was how
it prevented urinary tract infections.

I think one of the other major differences and one of the concepts that I think
people have to realise is that there are two things we tried to do for UTIs. One is
to try to prevent them. And the second is to try to treat them. Most of the studies
that have been done using cranberry products has been done to try to prevent
urinary tract infection.

What I think probably is true…I don't have proof of this but I have a feeling that
the Native Americans used it for this purpose as well and that's how the early
pilgrims and settlers did the same, which is that I believe cranberry juice probably
does have some anti-inflammatory effect or an effect that we're not quite sure
how it works, but it does reduce the burning sensation that women have when
they are developing a UTI. This is what many women anecdotally say cranberry
juice helps them for.

And so I think that when people start developing the UTI, so now we're going into
the realm of treatment, not prevention, that cranberry juice seems to ease those
symptoms. It does not treat the UTI, and I know women who have started taking
cranberry juice and the bladder infection goes on and progresses to a kidney
infection because the symptoms go away. But I think that that distinction is one
that is important for people to realise. And I think that that is somewhat blurred in
terms of the old wives' tales and the tradition of cranberry that exists in America
and therefore around the world as well. And what our study looked at really was
more about prevention, and that's what most of the studies that are in the
scientific literature are about, is about prevention of UTI with cranberry products.

Norman Swan: So tell us what you did in the study.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: So in our study I really tried to replicate the findings of
the first juice study that was in a strong way positive in older women. So this was
going back to 1994, a study published in the Journal of the American Medical
Association, JAMA, that looked at older women living in nursing homes and

assisted living facilities, and it looked at 10 ounces of cranberry juice cocktail to
prevent bacteria and white cells in the urine. The problem with cranberry juice is
that for many women it has a very acrid flavour, they can't drink the volume that
is necessary, they don't like the load of sugar that potentially could be with it. And
so for these reasons, even though that study was a positive study in that
population, many women are just unable to do that. And so for that reason in our
study I looked at the equivalent of 20 ounces of cranberry juice cocktail. So I
looked at two capsules. The capsule that we used had 36 milligrams of the
equivalent of proanthocyanidin, or a tannin which is in cranberry juice cocktail
that is thought to be the active ingredient in preventing UTIs…

Norman Swan: And in fact in the laboratory it has been shown to stop the
stickiness of the E. coli, the bug that causes the urinary tract infections, stops it
sticking to the surface lining of the urinary tract in the laboratory.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: That's exactly right. And so in the lab studies they have
been shown to inhibit binding to the bladder wall cells. In fact we used pilot data
from a previous study, and this is a compound we then used, that actually looks
at the urine of women who ingested various levels and doses of that active
ingredient and saw that there was decreased binding with increases in dose. And
so we ended up using 72 milligrams a pack, which was double the dose that was
shown the 1994 study, and the thought there was that in our pilot data we had
seen that 72 milligrams was more effective than 36 milligrams in these older
women. And my thought was that maybe by reducing the hydration we needed a
higher dose. And so that was the dose we then tested, and we enrolled 185
women who lived in nursing homes, followed them for one year and checked
their urine for bacteria and white cells in the urine every two months over the
course of that year.

Norman Swan: And you also checked them for symptomatic infections, in other
words whether they were getting burning and discomfort.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Yes exactly.

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: So we did check them for symptomatic infections as
well. One of the big challenges with that though is that in older women those

types of symptoms are very uncommon. So in our older overall findings we did
not find a difference or a reduction in bacteria or white blood cells in the urine of
these women over the course of one year.

Over that same one-year period of time, we only had 10 symptomatic UTIs in the
treatment group and 12 in the control group, so we really can't say too much
about that because we weren't powered to detect the difference for symptomatic
UTI. What we were powered for was to look at this difference between bacteria
and white cells in the urine.

Norman Swan: And when you say powered, you mean the number of people
that you had in your study versus the kind of effect that you were looking for.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Right. So to clarify that, whenever you are designing a
study you're trying to figure out what is the effect that we are anticipating these
cranberry capsules are going to have, and based on that '94 study we were
expecting a certain reduction, a 33% relative reduction in the amount of bacteria
and white cells in the urine. So based on that and based on the baseline
prevalence of bacteria and white cells in the urine to start with, we came up with
a calculation that we needed to have at least 180 patients in this trial. And we
were actually able to enrol 185, so a little bit more than what we were expecting.
Nevertheless, we still were not able to show a difference.

Norman Swan: So just to pick this apart just a little bit and briefly, you could
argue that not taking the juice loses the hydrating effect, the flushing effect. So in
other words maybe it is the cranberries plus flushing that works here rather than
the extract by itself. So I am a firm believer that the hydration is absolutely
necessary in terms of UTI prevention. Having said that, if we look at the bulk of
studies that have been done in multiple different populations, it's been shown that
cranberry juice products overall do not seem to be working. The body of
evidence would basically suggest, even in the juice studies, that cranberry versus
placebo juice alone even still did not have an effect. So one of the interesting
things is one study that was done looked at cranberry juice versus placebo. And
in both groups the rate of UTI went down.

Norman Swan: But it was because of the fluid.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Right, exactly. That would suggest that the hydration
alone was sufficient in that population. So one of the challenges of our study is
can we say that it is generalisable to all audiences, to all potential patients? And
the one thing I would say is we didn't test all potential groups. We did test older,
debilitated, frail women who were living in nursing homes. But aside from my
study, another review that looked at all the studies that have been done over the
last many years, so a Cochrane review that was done in 2012 actually also had
come to a similar conclusion that data to date does not suggest that cranberry
products are actually effective at preventing UTI.

Norman Swan: Which is a shame, because it would reduce the rate of use of
antibiotics.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Absolutely, and that's the main reason I did the study
in the first place is because nursing home residents are exposed to antibiotics so
frequently and they are at risk for infection, so much so that I was hoping that a
non-antimicrobial method would be possible at preventing UTIs in these
unfortunate women. But we did not find that. And hydration is challenging in
these women. Hydration, although it is strongly recommended, it is challenging.

Norman Swan: So where does that leave a younger woman, say, who is having
recurrent cystitis, driven nuts by it, if this is applicable to her, then cranberry
extract is probably not going to make a big difference to preventing cystitis. And
this is also a group of women who are overexposed to antibiotics, at least in the
Australian setting and I suspect in the American as well, the wrong antibiotics for
the wrong length of time. Just give us a potted story for the woman with recurrent
cystitis, because it's an incredibly painful condition.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: It absolutely is, and I think that although this study
really can't comment on that because the younger woman who is having
recurrent cystitis is a different type of patient. But what I would say is that for
those women, there are probably a few things that may help and are very low
risk. So for the younger woman, post coital voiding can help prevent having a
UTI.

Norman Swan: So going to the bathroom after you've had sex.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: That's correct, so going to the bathroom, urinating after
you've had sex can certainly be one thing that is easy to do and potentially could
reduce the number of UTIs you have. The second thing I have told many women
and I have seen anecdotally a lot of success is that women who really are strict
about the amount of fluids they take every day, so they carry around a large litre
water bottle and refill it as they are done and really push hydration all day long, I
have seen women that are very successful at preventing UTIs. It is a hard thing
to do, I won't deny that, but I think that that is a possibility.

Norman Swan: And if you do need antibiotics, I think that short courses…I think
that if you catch it early and you can take a short course, meaning a three-day
course to treat your urinary tract infection, that's probably your best case to
prevent getting a more complicated urinary tract infection. The other thing that we
do do sometimes for the younger woman who has had three UTIs in a year or
maybe two in six months and is just very debilitated by these recurrent cystitis
episodes is we can sometimes use a chronic suppressive antibiotic. It is not our
choice, it's not our agent of choice, it's not our method of choice. But if somebody
has really suffered a lot and really is looking for another method, that is one thing
that we can do.

Norman Swan: But nobody has researched the man in this, their partner, and
surely it makes sense that they are being reinfected by their partner, and we tend
to focus on investigations of the woman rather than looking at the partner to see
whether the partner is carrying something, and essentially it is a sexually
transmissible infection.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: That is certainly a possibility. I do think though that in
women the closeness of the rectum, the vagina, the urethra allows for the
bacteria that are in your own system to then colonise your own urethra and then
for the bacteria to travel up to the bladder and actually cause an infection. Having
said that, I do think that partners probably do share some of the same bacteria.
So it may or may not be that it is a sexually transmitted disease, rather that we
start seeing that couples share the same type of bacteria that is in the gut that
then can cause infections in the urinary system. And I think that that is the bigger
problem for younger women. I think younger women are often told to wipe from
front to back, this is the reason why, because again, you're trying to prevent
colonisation and infection with your own bacteria from getting into your own

bladder. And I think that's the real challenge for younger women who face this
problem.

I can speak for the United States, I'm not sure how this translates to Australia,
but in the United States, cranberry capsules are not a regulated industry, in the
sense that there is not clear oversight on the exact contents and what products
can say are in them and what they can say the effect is. I think that cranberry
juice, many women will tell me that it works for them. And for those who tell me
that I say continue using it. There is little downside to doing that.

Cranberry capsules on the other hand I think are a different category of product
because this is really an unregulated industry. It is an industry which has great
financial potential for companies, but it also is an industry where there is little
upside other than the health benefits. It's not like eating cranberry products or
drinking cranberry products or maybe at least you can enjoy them and maybe
say that there is a benefit in terms of the fact that you like ingesting them.
Capsules are actually very different in that way. And so I'm a little bit more
reluctant, especially based on our findings, to recommend women to take
capsules. Having said that, if they enjoy drinking cranberry juice or taking other
cranberry products, I encourage people to do that, even if they feel it does help
them in preventing UTIs, though the data would suggest it might not.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much indeed for joining us.

Manisha Juthani-Mehta: Thank you so much for having me.

Norman Swan: And supplements are not very well regulated here either.
Manisha Juthani-Mehta is an infectious physician and researcher at Yale
University's School of Medicine. And a longer version of that interview with a lot
more detail will be available for podcast from the Health Report's website. And
you are listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC news radio and CBC
radio across Canada.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a condition where the body's immune system attacks the
lining of joints, and if untreated can cause serious strife. It's more common than
you might think, and in recent years new medications have come onto the market
which specifically target the immune problem. The trouble is they cost tens of
thousands of dollars a year, when one of the alternative medications,

methotrexate, costs a tiny fraction. But according to a piece in today's Medical
Journal of Australia, doctors feed what's called the nocebo effect and convince
people that methotrexate is a dreadful drug. One of the authors is a
rheumatologist, Professor Inam Haq of the University of Sydney and he's with me
now. Welcome to the Health Report.

Inam Haq: Many thanks.

Norman Swan: So what is the nocebo effect?

Inam Haq: So I think that's when there's anticipation of adverse effects from a
medication through information that the patient may receive themselves or from
other people which may then reduce the efficacy of that drug or actually cause it
to be discontinued earlier than might be expected.

Norman Swan: As opposed to the placebo effect…

Inam Haq: Which is a positive.

Norman Swan: Where you expect positive results.

Inam Haq: That's right.

Norman Swan: What we're talking about here are called disease modifying anti-
rheumatoid drugs, or DMARDs, so these are actual ones that affect the disease
itself, and methotrexate is one of them. What are the myths around methotrexate
that doctors perpetuate in your view that make this nocebo effect come into
effect?

Inam Haq: The common one that patients can get, it could be from doctors, other
health professionals or from the internet or other colleagues, is that it's cancer,
that they are being treated for cancer. Because methotrexate at much higher
doses is used to treat various different types of cancer. But we use methotrexate
in a much lower dose, we use it by tablet or injection and we give it weekly.

Norman Swan: And that suggests then it's a very strong treatment.

Inam Haq: That's right, so patients can then think, oh my goodness, all my hair
will fall out and all the perceptions that people feel about what chemotherapy can
do.

Norman Swan: And there's also drug interactions which are not really a problem
which people might think is a problem which are also used in rheumatoid arthritis.

Inam Haq: That's right. So, often patients with rheumatoid arthritis who have
inflammation in their joints are given anti-inflammatory medications to help some
of the symptoms. And often a pharmacist and other health professionals say you
can't take those two drugs together. You can. You have to look at the patient
individually and make sure that there are no other reasons why they can't take it.
For example, if they had a stomach ulcer or whether their kidneys are functioning
all right. But overall there is nothing wrong with taking those drugs for short
periods of time.

Norman Swan: And then there is a notion that you don't want to actually share
bodily fluids with somebody on methotrexate because you might get the toxicity
too.

Inam Haq: Yes, that's right. The amount of drug that is actually excreted in bodily
tissues is negligible. So the chance of somebody getting methotrexate toxicity
from somebody else is highly unusual…

Norman Swan: Including pregnant women?

Inam Haq: So pregnant women shouldn't take the drug because it affects
dividing cells and can cause mutations in embryos and so on. So pregnant
women with arthritis shouldn't be taking the drug. But if you are a pregnant
woman in contact with somebody else, normal personal hygiene precautions are
absolutely fine.

Norman Swan: And you don't take this by injection, do you?

Inam Haq: Most people will have it via tablet once a week. For those people in
whom there are side-effects, most commonly nausea or abdominal discomfort,
you can give it by injection just under the skin.

Norman Swan: So there's a bit of a mythology about that too.

Inam Haq: That's right. It's interesting, because in other countries in the world
you can get it as a prepackaged injection, rather like a pen injection, which is
very simple, very easy and you can dispose of it very simply. In Australia that
isn't yet available, so it has to be prepared in a hospital, and it's prepared
according to…the standards of much higher doses of methotrexate that you
would use in chemotherapy. So there's a lot of fear around it.

Norman Swan: So what evidence is there that this mythology about
methotrexate…and we are just choosing this almost as an example, does create
side-effects and bad results?

Inam Haq: Well, I think I've had that in my personal practice. Since being in the
country I have had several patients who we've had a discussion around
methotrexate as the gold standard. It's an extremely effective drug, used well and
used correctly and used safely, at reducing joint inflammation and damage. And
I've given patients information and then we have…we get patients back to have a
discussion and they say, 'I'm not very keen, I've read about the side-effects, I've
looked things up,' or they may have heard from other people who are on the
drug. And that then leads to a rather difficult…you know, you're trying to catch up
the whole time, trying to emphasise the important positives of the drug and the
benefits versus some of the perceptions that people may have, that they've heard
from other people.

Norman Swan: I take it from your accent you worked in the UK.

Inam Haq: That's right.

Norman Swan: Were more people on methotrexate in the UK than here?

Inam Haq: No, I think it's probably a similar problem all over, yes.

Norman Swan: So we could save a lot of money here by putting people on
methotrexate if we set people's expectations correctly.

Inam Haq: I think we need to ensure that people go to the right sources of
information. For example, Arthritis Australia has fantastic patient related
information. I think we also need to educate our other healthcare providers,

general practitioners for example, practice nurses, to understand better that
methotrexate is not an unusual drug, it is actually the gold standard.

Norman Swan: But just in general, you can understand doctors being a bit
careful here because they've got to take informed consent and they want to
inform people about what side-effects are, but what you're saying is that by
informing people about side-effects you actually might create the side-effect.

Inam Haq: That's right. So it's actually quite a nuanced conversation that you
have to have with the patient around the severity and frequency of those effects
versus the undoubted and proven benefits of methotrexate at reducing joint
damage, inflammation and symptoms to allow that person to carry on with their
normal life.

Norman Swan: And some people have said that statins are the same thing, the
cholesterol lowering drugs, that you are led to expect muscle pain so you get
muscle pain.

Inam Haq: That's right, absolutely, you become hypervigilant as to what bodily
symptoms you have and may attribute them wrongly.

Norman Swan: So you've got to get that fine balance between informed consent
and realism.

Inam Haq: That's right. I think that's actually quite a difficult task and quite a
complex cognitive process.

Norman Swan: If you've got rheumatoid arthritis, do consider methotrexate…

Inam Haq: Very much so, it's a fantastic drug.

Norman Swan: And save the nation's economy. Inam Haq, thanks very much for
joining us.

Inam Haq: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Inam Haq is a rheumatologist at the University of Sydney. He's
also co-director of the Sydney University medical program.

There is pretty good evidence that if you are infected with a parasite in your early
childhood you are much less likely to develop asthma. The infection seems to
train your immune system to be less allergic. But most of us would probably
prefer asthma to a dose of worms. But that hasn't stopped a group of researchers
at James Cook University in Far North Queensland looking for a therapy based
on hookworms, and they may have found one.

Severine Navarro is a senior research fellow at James Cook and is in our Cairns
studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Severine Navarro: Hi, thank you so much for having me.

Norman Swan: So there's been…I've noticed just reading up for this, that in fact
there's been a randomised trial of in fact a certain kind of pin worm for asthma
already, the real worm.

Severine Navarro: Yes, but pin worm is different from hook worm…

Norman Swan: Sorry, whip worm rather, not pin worm, yes.

Severine Navarro: Yes, and whip worm as well, it was in a clinical trial, so for
inflammatory bowel disease. It was just not the right kind of worm.

Norman Swan: And not all worms…in terms of the epidemiology, looking at
populations, not all worm infections seem to reduce the risk of asthma. So it's not
every worm.

Severine Navarro: Absolutely, and some may actually even make it worse. But
what's interesting about the…

Norman Swan: Which ones make it worse, just in case we are exposed to them?

Severine Navarro: Oh, many different ones. Usually endemic countries where
you have multiple infections you will have different types of worms that will co-
infect the same host, and it's hard to pinpoint but some are definitely usually
emphasising the pro-allogenic type responses which are called T-helper 2s, and
all this will increase the discomfort and the allergenicity of different types of
allergens to the patient.

Norman Swan: And this is infection in the first year of life we're talking about,
isn't it?

Severine Navarro: No, actually it can be just about at any stage. There are
multiple studies that have been showing that children, young children but not
necessarily infants, when they get their worm removed with deworming medicine,
they start to have wheezing and sensitisation appearing. And this is when we
found a relationship between hook worm and allergy.

Norman Swan: In what way?

Severine Navarro: Well, that's the thing. So endemic areas where hook worm
infections are predominant, when you have migration of population, so that's
talking mainly about developing countries, but when you have the migration of
populations from rural to urban areas where they get access to better sanitation
and medication and get the opportunity to obviously get rid of their parasite
infections, a lot of people have suddenly been suffering from autoimmune
diseases and allergy.

Norman Swan: So that made you look at hook worm. And you've discovered this
chemical, this messenger, if you like, that seems to be the key.

Severine Navarro: Well, maybe not the key but a key for sure. It seems for the
public in general it will be definitely more appealing to take a pill than to just
swallow a capsule full of parasites.

Norman Swan: It takes a bit of thought, but you might be right.

Severine Navarro: The thing though is that in my personal opinion it's not just
adults that suffer from asthma, it's also very young children, and I can't imagine
having a young child on corticosteroids. If there is anything that we can do to
prevent this type of medication and help, I think that's the key.

Norman Swan: So this anti-inflammatory protein that you discovered, what does
it do?

Severine Navarro: Well, that's what's actually quite interesting about this protein,
and that's what…it's totally unprecedented, is that it seems like it is
reprogramming certain key cells that are defective in autoimmune and allergy

patients. And this sort of reprogramming is resetting the immune response the
right way and suppressing the immune responses that you have in allergen to
immunity.

Norman Swan: Protein obviously comes from the look worm. So obviously
you've got to test this further in animals and then in humans, but if this works, is it
going to be like hook worm infection where you've got to have it for life otherwise
if you stop this treatment you could get a nasty resurgence of your asthma or
allergy?

Severine Navarro: No, absolutely not. So the work that we've done, all the
preclinical work that we've already established, we've seen that a single course
of treatment which so far we've only established to be just a single uptake for 4 to
5 days will protect an organism for up to 14 weeks. So this was done in a study in
mice, so I don't know exactly how we can translate to humans yet. But that
means in terms of previous research done on small animals and asthma, it's
actually a really long time. So that would give the prospect of people just taking
maybe one little course of treatment for a few days, might be protected for
several months.

Norman Swan: And is there any prospect that this could treat autoimmune
disease, like diabetes and other conditions?

Severine Navarro: Possibly. We are currently investigating rheumatoid arthritis.
But the mechanism of action of this particular protein seems to indicate that it
might actually be applicable to multiple other pathologies.

Norman Swan: I hope you have patented it?

Severine Navarro: Oh, we have! But this is a great opportunity for us actually
because it's only with partnering with the industry or willing investors that we can
actually bring this molecule forward and hopefully sooner rather than later on the
market.

Norman Swan: Well, good luck with it, Severine, lots of people will be grateful for
a new treatment that might be so effective.

Severine Navarro: Thank you so much, and that's our reward.

Norman Swan: Thanks very much indeed. Severine Navarro is a senior
research fellow at James Cook University and was in our Cairns studio in Far
North Queensland.

Visiting Australia this week is a leading US gerontologist Dr Allen Power. He's
here to convince those caring for people with dementia that is often a better way
than drugs to control what can be very difficult behaviours. Allen Power is in our
Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Allen Power: Thank you so much for having me Norman.

Norman Swan: What are these behaviours?

Allen Power: Well, I'm going to step even away from the word 'behaviours'. I
think that what we have, what I learned, I've worked nearly two decades fulltime
in residential care, used antipsychotic and other drugs were people who are
distressed, and I think the predominant model we've been taught about dementia
has really focused on disease, neuropathology, and it's very reductionistic and
very focused on deficits. And as a result when somebody is distressed or
expresses themselves in other ways it is seen as a difficult behaviour, it is seen
as something that rests with that damaged brain, and that has led us into whole
paradigms like saying behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia that
really put the fault with the person. And if you really think that brain disease is the
root cause, then it's a slippery slope to using medications.

Norman Swan: So if it's not the disease, what's the cause?

Allen Power: Well, I had to step outside that and I had to say, you know,
neuropathology exists but it is part of a much larger thing and that is that it's
within the realm of the individual in how that individual experiences the disease
process. And so I focused on experience instead of just plain pathology, and
came to understand that there is so much more that we don't see, which is the
relational, historical and environmental factors around a person. And that really
we're talking about does the person have well-being, and are there things
between their illness and the way we care for them that may actually erode those
aspects of well-being.

Norman Swan: Be specific, tell us a story then.

Allen Power: A perfect example is if you or I living without a diagnosis of
dementia were brought to a shower room by somebody we had never met
before, our clothes were removed and we were showered in a way that maybe
we didn't prefer, with water that maybe had temperature not to our liking, that
would probably bother us. You or I might complain, we might refuse to continue.
A person with dementia who maybe can't remember or express themselves or
cope with the stressors, might shout or strike out. So there's a different response,
the dementia has become an enabler of their distress, but it wasn't the root
cause. The root cause was the way the shower was presented. And when we
blame it on the dementia, then we don't look deeper and we don't find what's
really missing.

Norman Swan: But what you've just described is probably more appropriate for
residential aged care. Plenty of people with dementia are at home and their
partners caring for them find that their behaviours can be very difficult;
aggression, wandering, sleep reversal, there are all sorts of things that happen
that when they desperately want to keep their loved one at home and up in aged
care because that's the only place for them. And as you say, the temptation is to
put them on very strong life-reducing drugs like antipsychotics.

Allen Power: Yes, so let's go to the home for a moment and let's take it out of
residential care. I've worked for years in the culture change field, mainly through
the Eden Alternative and Greenhouse models that came from the US, and what
we've learned is that an institution isn't a building, it's a mindset, it's a way of
operating. And when I look at dementia from the lens of these aspects of well-
being, and in this case I'm talking about seven domains—identity,
connectedness, security, autonomy, meaning, growth, joy.

Let's talk about autonomy for a moment. It is just as easy for a caring family
member who is taught the stigma that the person is fading away, that they are
incapable, to take away autonomy from a family member as well. So it is just as
likely that a person may react to that type of situation in their own home as they
do in a care home. And a perfect example of how institutional practices
transfer…one of the best ways to help a person who has memory loss is not to
rotate staff. It's constant in residential care that people are presented with, to
them, strangers to provide very personal care. Well, even in home care this
happens. My friend Sally Magnusson who is with BBC Glasgow wrote a book

about her mother's life, and interviewed the woman whose father lived at home,
and over the course of the year he had 106 different home health workers come
to his house to provide personal care. So these institutional practices happen
everywhere.

Norman Swan: But in an era where there are more and more people with
dementia, even though dementia rates are probably tailing off, is it practical to
give this sort of individual care, particularly in residential care?

Allen Power: It is practical but it requires…that's the third part. So I mentioned
the experiential focus, I mentioned the well-being focus, the third part in this
comes from my culture change backgrounds, this transforming the care system,
because it's not so much about uncaring people or even uneducated people, it's
about a system that still pushes them to focus on tasks, to focus on speed and to
blame the person instead of understanding all the subtle features of the care
environment that actually are causing more distress than the person needs to
have.

Norman Swan: So if your loved one is going into residential aged care, this is a
complete nightmare for people, how do you choose the right place for your loved
one, what are the hallmarks that you should be looking for in a residential aged
care facility?

Allen Power: I think the hallmarks are really to take…almost to close your eyes.
Forget about how pretty the lobby is. See what it feels like, see how people
speak to each other, see how they speak to people living with dementia and see
if they really are focused on the relationship, on the person. That really is where
the key is. The payoff is I work with organisations in the US that have actually not
only severely reduced but eliminated antipsychotic use. So if this really is just a
problem with brain disease, how can you explain somebody who goes from 30%
antipsychotics to zero and keeps it there for a long period of time.

Norman Swan: And ask them about the rosters to see about the consistency.
Allen Power, thank you.

Allen Power's books will be on our website. You've been listening to the Health
Report, I'm Norman Swan. See you next week.
